title: Sindhu Won. Lakshya Lost. Srikanth Lost. India's Indonesia Open Started With One Player Carrying the Entire Country.
excerpt: PV Sindhu, back in the world top ten after 954 days, beat Busanan Ongbamrungphan for a 21st time. Lakshya Sen and Kidambi Srikanth both fell in the opening round of the Super 1000 event in Jakarta.
body:
She was out of the world's top ten for 954 days. On Tuesday, at the Istora Senayan in Jakarta, PV Sindhu looked like someone who had no intention of leaving again.

The two-time Olympic medallist opened her Indonesia Open 2026 campaign with a straight-games victory over Thailand's Busanan Ongbamrungphan, winning 25-23, 21-16 in a match that ran 51 minutes and felt like a statement. It was Sindhu's 21st win in 22 career meetings with the Thai shuttler — and her 11th consecutive — a head-to-head record so lopsided it borders on dominance by default.

## Back in the Top Ten, and Looking Up

The win came just days after Sindhu re-entered the BWF top ten for the first time since 2023, capping a quiet but steady climb back through the rankings on the strength of back-to-back quarterfinal finishes and a refusal to do anything halfway. In Jakarta, that trajectory was visible from the first rally.

The opening game was a fight. Sindhu built a 19-15 lead with aggressive net play and sharp cross-court smashes, but Busanan clawed back, forcing extra points before Sindhu steadied herself to close it 25-23. The second game was more emphatic. Sindhu led from the start, attacking the backhand corner relentlessly and closing out 21-16 with the kind of controlled aggression that made her a world champion.

She now faces a potential Round of 16 clash against World No. 1 An Se-young of South Korea — the reigning Olympic champion and a player against whom Sindhu holds a daunting 0-9 record. An defeated Sindhu in the Singapore Open quarterfinals just last week. The question is no longer whether Sindhu can compete at this level but whether she can crack the code against the one player who has her number.

## A Bad Day for Indian Men's Singles

If Sindhu carried the flag, the men's singles contingent dropped it. Lakshya Sen, India's highest-ranked male shuttler, lost 19-21, 16-21 to home favourite Alwi Farhan — a player who upset World No. 1 Shi Yu Qi at the Singapore Open last week and is fast becoming a gatekeeper at major events. Sen never established the tempo needed to contain Farhan's speed and was second to every rally in the second game.

Former World No. 1 Kidambi Srikanth also exited in the opening round, falling 19-21, 15-21 to Japan's Yushi Tanaka. Srikanth showed glimpses of vintage quality — a few whip-fast smashes and deceptive drop shots — but unforced errors in critical moments have become a recurring feature of his game, and the 32-year-old could not sustain the intensity.

Malvika Bansod was outclassed 21-12, 21-10 by seventh seed Pornpawee Chochuwong in the women's singles.

## The Bright Spots: Doubles

In the men's doubles, Hariharan Amsakarunan and MR Arjun produced the upset of the day, defeating Malaysia's experienced pair of Nur Mohd Azriyn Ayub and 2016 Olympic medallist Tan Wee Kiong 21-18, 21-10. The Indian duo was compact and clinical — they competed in the first game and demolished their opponents in the second, finishing in just 33 minutes.

Meanwhile, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty arrived in Jakarta as defending Singapore Open champions and among the tournament's strongest medal hopes. The pair's title-winning run in Singapore last week — their first Super 750 title — gave them momentum heading into the Super 1000 event. Their draw opens in the second round.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian-origin fans in the US, UK, and Canada, the Indonesia Open is more than a tournament — it is a barometer. Sindhu's resurgence matters because she remains the most globally recognisable Indian shuttler, and her return to the top 10 carries symbolic weight. If she can find a way past An Se-young — even once — it would be among the biggest results of her post-Olympic career.

The men's singles crisis runs deeper. Lakshya Sen and Srikanth both exiting in the first round of a Super 1000 event is not the preparation India needs with the BWF World Championships in New Delhi less than two months away. For NRIs who grew up watching Saina Nehwal and Sindhu turn India into a badminton nation, the contrast between the women's consistency and the men's fragility is hard to ignore.
author: Diaspora Desk
